newsitem.title: ITALY: "Textbook" papal appendix surgery excludes tumour. [CORRECTED 16:45 GMT]
newsitem.headline: "Textbook" papal appendix surgery excludes tumour. [CORRECTED 16:45 GMT]

text.p: Pope John Paul (corrects to restore dropped name "Paul") had his appendix removed on Tuesday and doctors said the "textbook" operation had been a perfect success and showed that the Roman Catholic leader was not suffering from another tumour.
Francesco Crucitti, chief surgeon at the Gemelli hospital, told a packed news conference the operation had allowed doctors to "exclude, yet again" the presence of other diseased tissue.
Crucitti, grilled by journalists despite his opening statement, was firm in ruling out another tumour.
"I exclude it in the most categorical way. There are no secrets...it was exactly what the pre-operative tests showed," he said. "He has never had any other growth (since 1992)."
A Vatican statement last month that three bouts of fever the 76-year-old Pope has suffered since Christmas had been caused by recurrent inflammation of the appendix had met with scepticism.
Some doctors had speculated that the Polish-born Pope might have a new tumour after one the size of an orange was removed in 1992 as it was starting to turn malignant.
The Pope spent about two hours in the operating theatre but the surgery itself lasted 50 minutes. Doctors said the Pope had shown no ill effects during surgery or from the anaesthetic.
"Everything went okay, perfectly okay (and) very quickly," cardiologist Attilio Maseri, who monitored the Pope's heart during surgery, told Reuters.
Preliminary tissue tests after the operation, which left the Pope with about 10 stitches, also confirmed the diagnosis of "recurring episodes of inflammtion of the appendix".
A bulletin signed by Crucitti and five other specialists said doctors also cleared up some intestinal "adhesions", when normally separate tissues or loops of intestine, stick together.
Adhesions, which can be painful, are common in patients who have abdominal surgery. The Pope had such surgery twice in 1981 after an assassination attempt and to remove the tumour in 1992.
Crucitti sidestepped a barrage of questions by reporters who have laid seige to the Gemelli about something else that is clearly ailing the Pope -- a violently trembling left hand.
The Vatican has not denied reports that the trembling, and facial rigidity and a stooped gait, could be signs of Parkinson's Disease or a similar neurological disorder.
"There are specialists who are following him. This is not my field," Crucitti said.
The Pope, who had asked Catholics to pray for him before entering hospital on Sunday evening, heard mass in his special 10th floor suite at the Gemelli before the operation.
He appeared relaxed and smiled at nurses and security guards on his way to the theatre and Crucitti said the Pope had also been alert on emerging from anaesthetic.
"When he came round he greeted everybody and thanked them. He was calm throughout," he said.
He expected the "Pilgrim Pope," who has travelled over one million kilometres in 74 trips abroad, to be confined to bed for only a day and said he might leave hospital before next Tuesday.

At the Vatican, chief spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said the Pope had asked to hear the official medical report, which had been read to him by a nun. "He got the news just a little before you," Navarro-Valls told reporters.
The Vatican also issued the report on the Internet.

Navarro-Valls said hundreds of get-well messages, many from non-Christians, "show that the Pope is not only the leader of a Church but of all humanity." One was sent by Mehmet Ali Agca, the Turk who shot the Pope in 1981.
The Pontiff, who next week will mark the 18th anniversary of his 1978 election as the first non-Italian Pope in 455 years, has kept up a gruelling schedule despite frailty and old age.
Crucitti timidly suggested: "If I could venture my own opinion, I think that the Pope should rest more."
